q: 1. The deformation of a bar under its own weight is ............. the deformation, if the same body is subjected to a direct load equal to weight of the body.
explain: Self-weight elongation (wl²/2E) is exactly half of the elongation caused by an equivalent direct end load equal to the total weight (Wl/AE), since self-weight effectively acts as if applied at the centroid on average.

q: 2. The elongation of a conical bar under its own weight is ............. that of prismatic bar of the same length.
explain: Due to the tapering cross-section reducing internal force build-up, a conical bar's self-weight elongation is one-third that of an equivalent prismatic bar of the same length.

q: 3. The length of a conical bar is l, diameter of base is d and weight per unit volume is w. It is fixed at its upper end and hanging freely. The elongation of the bar under the action of its own weight will be
explain: For a conical bar under self-weight, integrating gives an elongation of wl²/6E, consistent with it being one-third of the prismatic bar's wl²/2E value.

q: 4. Strain rosetters are used to
explain: Strain rosettes consist of multiple strain gauges arranged to measure linear (normal) strains in different directions at a point, from which principal strains can be derived.

q: 5. The maximum stress produced in a bar of tapering section is at
explain: For a given axial load, stress = Force/Area, so the smaller cross-sectional area at the smaller end of a tapering bar experiences the maximum stress.

q: 6. Modular ratio of the two materials is the ratio of
explain: Modular ratio, used in composite section analysis, is defined as the ratio of the moduli of elasticity of the two materials involved.

q: 7. The shear modulus of most materials with respect to the modulus of elasticity is
explain: For typical materials with Poisson's ratio around 0.25–0.3, the relation G = E/[2(1+μ)] gives G somewhat less than half of E.

q: 8. A rod is enclosed centrally in a tube and the assembly is tightened by rigid washers. If assembly is subjected to a compressive load, then
options: both rod and tube are under compression
tube is under tension and rod is under compression
explain: Since the rigid washers force the rod and tube to shorten together under the applied compressive load, both components share and resist the load in compression.

q: 9. When a bar is subjected to a change of temperature and its deformation is prevented, stress induced in the bar is
explain: When thermal expansion/contraction of a restrained bar is prevented, the resulting internal stress is generically termed thermal stress (which may be tensile or compressive depending on direction of temperature change).

q: 10. A steel bar of 5 mm is heated from 15°C to 40°C and it if free to expand. The bar will induce
explain: If the bar is completely free to expand (unrestrained), no internal stress develops regardless of temperature change, since there is no resistance to the deformation.

q: 11. When a bar is cooled to −5°C, it will develop
explain: As with heating, if the bar is free (unrestrained) while being cooled, it can contract freely and no internal stress is induced.

q: 12. A bar of copper and steel form a composite system, which is heated to a temperature of 40. The stress induced in the copper bar will be
explain: Since copper has a higher coefficient of thermal expansion than steel, in a bonded composite bar heated together, copper is restrained from expanding as much as it wants by the steel, inducing compressive stress in the copper.

q: 13. When a circular bar tapering uniformly from diameter d1 at one end to diameter d2 at the other end, is subjected to an increase in temperature (t), then the thermal stress induced is
explain: For a fully restrained tapering bar under temperature rise t, the standard thermal stress relation (as given in the source) is expressed as a·t·E·d1/d2, matching option (a).

q: 14. The Poisson's ratio for steel varies from
explain: The typical Poisson's ratio for steel lies in the range 0.23 to 0.27 (commonly cited as ~0.25–0.3, with 0.23–0.27 as this book's stated range).

q: 15. The Poisson's ratio for cast iron varies from
explain: Cast iron typically has a somewhat higher/varying Poisson's ratio range of about 0.25 to 0.33 compared to steel.

q: 16. When a bar of length l, width b and thickness t is subjected to a pull of P, its
options: length increases, width and thickness decreases
length decreases, width and thickness increases
explain: Under axial tension (a pull), the bar elongates (length increases) while due to Poisson's effect it contracts laterally (width and thickness decrease).

q: 17. When a bar of length l, width b and thickness t is subjected to a push of P, its
options: length increases, width and thickness decreases
length decreases, width and thickness increases
explain: Under axial compression (a push), the bar shortens (length decreases) while it expands laterally due to Poisson's effect (width and thickness increase).

q: 18. The ratio of bulk modulus to Young's modulus for a Poisson's ratio of 0.25 will be
explain: Using K/E = 1/[3(1−2μ)], substituting μ=0.25 gives K/E = 1/[3(0.5)] = 2/3.

q: 19. In the case of T section, the maximum bending stress will occur at
explain: Since a T-section's neutral axis is closer to the flange, the farthest extreme fibre (in the web, at the bottom) experiences the maximum bending stress.

q: 20. The line showing the variations of stress function at a given point due to a unit load moving on a span is known as
explain: This is the formal definition of an influence line. It tracks how a single 'unit' load affects one specific point as that load changes position.

q: 21. The neutral axis of any section is
options: the axis passing through middle point of the height
the line of intersection of neutral plane with cross-section
the axis about which the moment of inertia is minimum
explain: The neutral axis is defined as the line of intersection between the neutral plane (zero-strain plane) of the beam and its cross-section.

q: 22. Which of the following materials will have the highest Young's Modulus?
explain: Among the listed materials, mild steel has the highest Young's modulus (~200 GPa), significantly higher than brass, copper, or timber.

q: 23. Creep of a material is
options: continued deformation with time under sustained loading
disappearance of deformation on removal of load
explain: Creep is defined as the gradual, continued deformation of a material over time while subjected to a constant sustained load, even below the yield stress.

q: 24. What is tenacity?
explain: Tenacity is the technical term for the ultimate tensile strength of a material.

q: 25. At ordinary temperatures, how is the yield point affected with rate of loading?
explain: At normal (ordinary) temperatures, the yield point of typical metals is not greatly affected by moderate changes in loading rate.

q: 26. If all the dimensions of prismatic bar are doubled, then the maximum stress produced in it under its own weight will
explain: Self-weight stress at the base = weight/area ∝ (volume×density)/area ∝ length (since volume/area ∝ length for a scaled bar); doubling all dimensions doubles the length, hence doubling this self-weight stress.

q: 27. Limiting values of Poisson's ratio are
explain: From thermodynamic stability requirements for isotropic elastic materials, Poisson's ratio must lie between −1 and 0.5.

q: 28. The ratio of the stresses produced by a suddenly applied load and by a gradually applied load on a bar is
explain: A suddenly applied load produces twice the stress (and deflection) of the same load applied gradually, a classic impact-loading result.

q: 29. Maximum strain theory for the failure of material at the elastic limit is known as
explain: The maximum strain theory of failure is also known as St. Venant's theory.

q: 30. Maximum shear stress theory for the failure of a material at the elastic limit is known as
explain: The maximum shear stress theory of failure is also called Guest's theory or Tresca's theory.

q: 31. Maximum principal stress theory for the failure of a material at elastic point is known as
explain: The maximum principal stress theory of failure is also known as Rankine's theory.

q: 32. Total strain energy theory for the failure of a material at the elastic limit is known as
explain: The total strain energy theory of failure is also known as Haig's theory (Beltrami's theory).

q: 33. A localized compressive stress at the area of contact between two members is known as
explain: A localized compressive stress at the contact area between two members (such as at a bearing or joint) is termed crushing (bearing) stress.

q: 34. Principle plane is a plane on which the shear stress is
explain: A principal plane is defined as a plane on which the shear stress is zero, and only normal (principal) stress acts.

q: 35. The extremities of any diameter on Mohr's circle represent
options: normal and shear stresses on a plane
explain: Each point on Mohr's circle represents the normal and shear stress combination on a particular plane; the two ends of any diameter represent stresses on two mutually perpendicular planes.

q: 36. The percentage of elongation of a material with applied direct tensile test is:
explain: While percentage elongation is a measure of 'Ductility', the answer key provided marks 'Rupture' (c). In testing context, elongation is measured until the point of rupture/failure.

q: 37. If 'S' is the axial acting on an element 'ds' of a structural member with cross sectional area 'A' and modulus of elasticity 'E' the total strain energy of the member on account of axial force 'S' is given by
explain: The standard formula for axial strain energy is $U = \int  rac{P^2}{2AE} dx$.

q: 38. If the span of real beam is l, the span of the corresponding conjugate beam is
explain: In the conjugate beam method, the conjugate beam has the same span (length) as the real beam; only the support conditions and loading (M/EI diagram) change.

q: 39. The loading on the conjugate beam will be
options: loading on the real beam divided by EI
B.M. diagram divided by SF diagram
explain: The conjugate beam method loads the conjugate beam with the M/EI diagram of the real beam (bending moment diagram divided by flexural rigidity EI).

q: 40. The stress due to temperature change in a member depends on
options: supporting conditions at the two ends
explain: Thermal stress develops only if expansion/contraction is restrained; hence it depends fundamentally on the support/end conditions (degree of restraint), not on length or area directly.

q: 41. The percentage elongation of a material from a direct tensile test indicates
explain: Percentage elongation (increase in gauge length at fracture) is the standard measure of a material's ductility.

q: 42. The percentage reduction in area of a member from a direct tension test indicates
explain: Percentage reduction in cross-sectional area at fracture, like percentage elongation, is a standard measure of ductility.

q: 43. The Poisson's ratio is the ratio of
options: Yong's modulus elasticity to modulus of rigidity
explain: Poisson's ratio is, by definition, the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal (axial) strain under uniaxial loading.

q: 44. The equation connection Yong's modulus (E) Poisson's (1/m) and Modulus of Rigidity (C), is
explain: The standard elastic relation connecting Young's modulus E, modulus of rigidity C(G), and Poisson's ratio (1/m) is E = 2C(1 + 1/m).

q: 45. The strain energy stored in a body, when suddenly loaded, is ............. the strain energy stored when same load is applied gradually.
explain: A suddenly applied load causes twice the stress/deformation of a gradual load, and since strain energy ∝ (deformation)², the stored energy becomes four times as much.

q: 46. To avoid any possibility of tension occurring in masonry structures, the resultant of various forces at any level must through
options: middle third of the width or depth of the section
explain: The 'middle third rule' requires the resultant force to pass within the middle third of the section width/depth to prevent tensile stress in masonry (which cannot resist tension).

q: 47. Strain in concrete at zero stress is called :
explain: Creep is the time-dependent deformation of concrete under sustained load, often continuing after stress is removed.

q: 48. The stress at which extension of a material takes place more quickly as compared to the increase in load, is called
explain: The yield point is defined as the stress at which strain (extension) increases disproportionately faster than the applied load/stress.

q: 49. Every material obeys the Hooke's law within its
explain: Hooke's law (stress directly proportional to strain) strictly holds only up to the limit of proportionality on the stress-strain curve.

q: 50. The law which states, "Within elastic limits strain produced is proportional to the stress producing it", is known as
explain: This statement is the definition of Hooke's Law.
